texts.title: Measuring the depth of the sea

paragraphs.text: For most of history, the depth of the sea was known only where it mattered to sailors, which meant close to the shore. A navigator approaching a harbour needed to know whether there was enough water beneath the keel, and the method used to find out changed very little for two thousand years: a weight of lead was attached to a marked rope, lowered over the side until it touched the bottom, and hauled back while the length of line was counted. The underside of the weight was often hollowed out and filled with tallow, so that a sample of sand, shell or mud stuck to it, and experienced pilots could recognise a stretch of coast by the texture of its seabed alone.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: In deep water the method became almost useless. Lowering a line several kilometres took hours, the ship drifted while it was being done, and currents pulled the rope into a curve so that the length paid out overstated the true depth. When nineteenth-century expeditions began to take soundings in the open ocean, each measurement could occupy most of a day, and a ship crossing an ocean might return with a few hundred numbers scattered along its route. The maps drawn from them showed broad basins and gentle slopes, largely because there was nothing in the data to show anything else.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The laying of telegraph cables across the ocean floor gave the work an economic purpose. A cable company needed to know whether the route crossed sharp ridges that might break the line or deep trenches that would require more cable than had been manufactured, and it was prepared to pay for surveys that governments had not. Wire replaced rope, which reduced the drag and allowed a sounding to be completed faster, and machines were built to wind the wire back. The surveys also brought up samples of the bottom, and the discovery that the deep seabed was covered in the remains of microscopic organisms opened a field of research that had little to do with telegraphy.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Sound transformed the subject in the early twentieth century. Rather than lowering anything, a ship could send a pulse of sound downwards and time the echo; since the speed of sound in water was known, the interval gave the depth. An echo sounder could take a measurement every few seconds while the ship continued at normal speed, so a single voyage now produced a continuous line of depths instead of scattered points. The profiles that resulted showed a seabed far more rugged than anyone had supposed, including a mountain range running down the middle of the Atlantic, whose existence had been suspected from earlier soundings but whose scale had not.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Continuous profiles were still only lines across a very large area, and the gaps between them had to be filled by interpolation. The next step was to send out many beams at once in a fan beneath the ship, so that each pass covered a strip of seabed several times as wide as the water was deep. Such multibeam systems, developed first for military purposes, produce detailed images rather than profiles, and they revealed features ranging from underwater landslides to the tracks left by icebergs grinding along the bottom during past cold periods. They are, however, slow in absolute terms, because even a wide strip is narrow compared with an ocean.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Satellites offered a shortcut that seemed at first to make ships unnecessary. The surface of the sea is not perfectly flat: the gravity of a large underwater mountain draws water towards it, raising the surface above it by a small but measurable amount. By measuring the height of the sea surface precisely from orbit, scientists could infer the shape of the bottom across the whole ocean in a few years. The results are global but coarse, since features smaller than a few kilometres produce no detectable bump, and the method depends on assumptions about the density of the rock beneath the seabed that are not always correct.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The result is a strange imbalance. At the resolution most scientists would regard as useful, only around a quarter of the ocean floor has been mapped directly, while the surfaces of several other planets are known in greater detail. An international project now aims to complete a high-resolution map of the whole seabed, relying partly on new survey vessels and partly on data already collected but never shared, since a large quantity of measurements sits in the archives of companies and navies. Some of that data is commercially sensitive, and persuading its owners to release it has proved at least as difficult as the survey work itself.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The practical reasons for finishing the map are numerous. Tsunami models depend on the shape of the seabed, since the height of a wave arriving at a coast is strongly influenced by the terrain it crosses on the way. Fisheries, the placement of cables and the prediction of how ocean currents carry heat all rely on the same information. Yet the argument that is made most often is simpler: the ocean covers most of the planet, and it seems odd that a species able to photograph distant moons should still be relying on estimates for the landscape beneath its own seas.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: How the pencil got its lead

paragraphs.text: The pencil is so ordinary that it is easy to forget it was once a technological puzzle. Its core is not lead and never has been; the name survives from a time when a soft grey mineral found in northern England was thought to be a form of lead, and the misunderstanding has outlasted the knowledge that corrected it by more than two centuries. The mineral was graphite, a form of pure carbon, and for a long period a single deposit supplied most of the graphite of sufficient quality to write with. It was so valuable that the mine was guarded, opened only for a few weeks each year, and flooded when not in use to discourage theft.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Early pencils were made by sawing the solid graphite into thin sticks and wrapping them in string or setting them into a groove in a strip of wood. The result wrote well but was expensive and depended entirely on the one deposit, whose output was deliberately restricted to keep prices high. Attempts to use the powdered graphite left over from sawing, by mixing it with glue or sulphur and pressing it into shape, produced cores that were brittle, scratchy or both. For most of the eighteenth century, a country without access to the English deposit had no satisfactory pencil. Smuggling of the English material was common enough to be punished severely.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The solution, when it came, owed much to war. Cut off from English supplies at the end of the eighteenth century, France needed pencils for its administration and its army, and a French engineer was asked to find a substitute. He found that powdered graphite of modest quality, mixed with fine clay and water, could be formed into rods and fired in a kiln, rather as pottery is. The clay bound the graphite particles together, and the resulting core was strong enough to sharpen and smooth enough to write with, even though the graphite in it would have been useless on its own.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The method had a consequence that its inventor may not have anticipated: it made the hardness of the pencil adjustable. More clay produced a harder core that made a pale, fine line and wore away slowly, while more graphite produced a softer, darker line that wore away quickly. Manufacturers began to offer grades, and the letter-and-number systems still printed on pencils describe, in effect, the proportion of clay to graphite. Draughtsmen, who needed fine lines that would not smudge, and artists, who wanted deep shading, could now buy tools made for their particular purposes. Some grades became so closely associated with particular trades that a draughtsman could often be identified by the hard pencil kept behind his ear.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The modern manufacturing process remains recognisably the one developed two centuries ago. Graphite and clay are ground together with water for many hours until the mixture is completely uniform, since any lump would later cause the core to break. The resulting paste is pressed through a narrow opening to form a continuous thread, which is cut into lengths and dried. The dried rods are then fired at a temperature of around a thousand degrees, after which they are soaked in hot wax, which fills the tiny pores left by the firing and allows the core to glide across paper rather than scratch it.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The wooden case is made separately and is, in its own way, as carefully engineered. Blocks of a soft, straight-grained wood are cut into thin slats, and parallel grooves are cut into each slat. The cores are laid in the grooves, a second grooved slat is glued on top to form a sandwich, and the sandwich is then cut apart into individual pencils and shaped, usually into six sides so that the pencil does not roll off a sloping desk. The choice of wood matters because the pencil must be sharpened easily without splitting, and the preferred species became scarce enough in the twentieth century that manufacturers turned to plantations and substitutes.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The appearance of the pencil has also been shaped by commerce. The practice of painting the case a strong yellow is usually traced to a manufacturer that wanted its product associated with the high-quality graphite then arriving from a mine in the east, where the colour carried connotations of luxury; competitors copied the colour, and it became the default in several countries. Whether the story is complete is uncertain, but the fact that a colour was chosen to signal the quality of an invisible core illustrates how much of the design of the pencil concerns what the buyer believes rather than what the pencil does.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Digital devices have not removed the pencil from use, and in some settings they have not even reduced it. Carpenters, surgeons marking the skin before an operation, and students in examinations that forbid pens continue to rely on it, partly because a pencil works in any orientation, at any temperature and without a battery, and partly because its mark can be erased. Annual production is still measured in billions. The mineral that was once guarded in a single English valley is now mined and manufactured on several continents, and the technical problem that occupied engineers for two centuries has become so thoroughly solved that it is no longer noticed.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Should extinct species be brought back?

paragraphs.text: The idea of reviving extinct animals has moved in a few decades from science fiction to grant applications. No one has yet produced a living individual of a species that has disappeared completely, and the most ambitious projects aim not at exact copies but at modern animals edited to resemble their lost relatives. Nevertheless, the prospect is close enough that it has begun to shape discussions about conservation, and it deserves an assessment that goes beyond enthusiasm about the technology or disgust at the ambition. The question worth asking is not whether it can be done but what, if it were done, it would be for.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The technical route is more modest than the headlines suggest. Genetic material from extinct animals survives, when it survives at all, in fragments, and no complete working genome has been recovered for any species that died out long ago. What researchers can do is identify the genes that distinguished the extinct animal from its closest living relative and alter those genes in the cells of the living species. The result would be a new animal carrying some of the traits of the old one, and Anna Lindqvist, a geneticist, insists that it should be described honestly as such rather than as a resurrected species, since an animal is shaped by its upbringing and environment as well as by its genes.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The most persuasive argument for the work concerns ecosystems rather than individual species. Some extinct animals performed functions that nothing now performs: large grazers that kept grassland open, for example, or seed-dispersing birds whose disappearance left certain trees without a way of spreading. Mateo Guerrero, an ecologist, argues that restoring the function matters more than restoring the species, and that an edited animal able to perform the lost role would be valuable even if it were not an exact replica. He accepts that the same function might sometimes be achieved more cheaply by introducing a living species from elsewhere. Grassland that is no longer grazed, for instance, can turn to scrub within a few decades, whatever animal eventually does the grazing.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Critics point first to cost. Conservation budgets are small and are already insufficient to protect many species that still exist, and Samira Haddad, who advises on biodiversity funding, argues that every sum spent on reviving a lost animal is a sum not spent on preventing the next loss. She does not claim that the money would automatically be diverted from existing programmes, since some of it comes from private donors attracted precisely by the novelty. Her concern is rather that a public told extinction can be reversed may become less willing to pay for measures that prevent it, a risk that is difficult to measure but plausible.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: A second objection concerns the animals themselves. The first individuals of any revived species would be born without parents of their own kind, and in social species a great deal of behaviour is learned rather than inherited. A young animal raised by a surrogate of a related species, or by humans, might lack the skills its ancestors acquired from their elders, and Haddad and others have questioned whether it is acceptable to create a creature whose welfare cannot be predicted. Supporters reply that captive breeding of endangered species raises similar issues and is not usually regarded as wrong for that reason.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: There is also the question of where a revived animal would live. The habitats that supported many extinct species have been transformed by farming, building and changes in climate, and releasing an animal into a landscape that no longer suits it would achieve little. Oliver Pratt, who works on the reintroduction of existing species, notes that even well-studied reintroductions frequently fail in their first attempts, and that a species whose behaviour is known only from bones and historical accounts would present far greater uncertainty. He argues that any revival project should be required to identify a suitable habitat before, rather than after, the first animal is produced.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The public response to these projects is itself a factor. Revival attracts attention and money that ordinary conservation struggles to obtain, and some conservationists argue that this attention could be channelled towards protecting habitats that would benefit living species as well as revived ones. Others fear the opposite: that a spectacular success would reinforce the belief that technology can repair any damage, making careful protection seem less urgent. Both effects are possible, and which predominates would probably depend on how the projects are presented. Several projects have been launched with campaigns that emphasise charismatic animals rather than ecological roles, which suggests that the presentation is not always designed with conservation in mind.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: On balance, the case for reviving lost species is strongest where it is narrowest. An edited animal intended to restore a specific ecological function, released into a habitat that has been prepared for it and supported by funding that does not compete with the protection of living species, would be a defensible experiment. A project aimed at producing a famous extinct animal for its own sake would not. The distinction is not always made by those promoting the work, and it is the one that regulators, funders and the public should insist on before the first animal is born.
paragraphs.label: H
